subtopic: IMMIGRATION
IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the
main reasons why Canadians have lost confidence in the Government is the inability of the Conservatives to keep the promises they made to the Canadian people.
Recently, the Canadian government staged a refugee immigration crisis and it tried to manipulate public opinion to make their situation even worse.
Immigrant refugees were used by the Conservatives for political reasons, like the debate on capital punishment. This kind of tactic is as irresponsible as their campaign promises.
The conservatives promised to give us a fair and equitable immigration policy, to introduce training programs to make immigration offices outside the country better informed, to help immigrants acquire a thorough knowledge of one of the official languages and to make Canadians more aware of our cultural mosaic.
Mr. Speaker, these actions and promises are an insult to the intelligence of Canadians, and I regret the Government having taken this position.

subtopic: U.S.S.R.-FATE OF JEWISH CITIZENS
U.S.S.R.-FATE OF JEWISH CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, Mrs. Ida Milgrom, the 78 year old mother of Anatoly Shcharansky, visited Ottawa to urge politicians to increase the pressure on the U.S.S.R. to let people leave that country. Mrs.
Milgrom scoffed at Gorbachev's new policy of openness, or glasnost in Russian, because thousands of Jews have been waiting years to obtain their exit visas.
She asked for our specific help to free Ida Nudel, a longtime refusnik whose health is failing due to years of frustration and persecution.
Mrs. Milgrom also highlighted the struggle of refusniks Lev and Inna Elbert who have been waiting 11 years for exit visas and who finally, out of despair and frustration, began a hunger strike on March 5.
Today we welcome over 100 Jewish students from across Canada from Network Canada and their President, Michael Zeldman. They are in the nation's capital to visit over 40 Members of Parliament to stress the desperate plight of thousands of refusniks and prisoners of conscience in the U.S.S.R.
Regrettably, at this point in time glasnost remains a misleading, deceitful word, totally empty of substance and commitment.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian youth still await the Government's youth program, but they have not had to wait for New Democrats whose youth task force recommendations, formulated largely by youth, became our policy last weekend.
The Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) consumes himself in defensiveness over the not so Hot 100. He is now joined by the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg). This is the handbook which claims to list 100 programs, services, and resources financed by the feds for youth.
All the hot and angry letters to me from the Minister or statements in the House will not change the fact that too many of the programs listed in the booklet, in an effort to make the Government look good, are neither financed by the feds nor designed specifically for youth.
The Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni was right about one thing-New Democrats support Canadian culture to which honesty, especially for youth, is fundamental.
The Government promised a youth policy, and promised and promised and promised, and a broken promise is a form of dishonesty. If the Government wants something really hot, we have something to warm even a hard Tory heart-the New Democratic Party youth policy.
March 19, 1987

NATIONAL PAROLE BOARD	UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE

Mr. Speaker, less than a month ago Canadians were shocked to learn that a man convicted of two rape-murders and an attempted rape-murder had been released on an unescorted day pass by the National Parole Board.
Last week we were shocked even more to learn that the police were placing bodyguards around a judge, a crown attorney, and the witnesses to an attempted murder, because the National Parole Board had released the man convicted of that crime after he served only a third of his sentence.
Worse yet, the Chairman of the National Parole Board admitted last week that his board does not have any clear criteria to use when granting a parole. No wonder, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians see the National Parole Board's decisions as arbitrary, inconsistent, and often downright reckless. No wonder the Minister of Justice and the Attorney General of Ontario admit that Canadians have lost confidence in the justice system. The parole system must be changed, and it must be changed now.

subtopic: EARLY RETIREES' RIGHT TO BENEFITS
EARLY RETIREES' RIGHT TO BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 35,000 early retirees in Canada, including 13,000 in Quebec, won another victory yesterday. After waiting for a year and two months, the government has finally decided to admit these people were right. However, there is some thing I think the government should know. I spoke to the people in charge of ARSAC in Quebec, Mr. Cloutier and Mrs. Jeanne Lalanne. Monday there will be a meeting in Montreal and Thursday one in Quebec City, and the people of ARSAC, our early retirees, will persevere until they have their unemployment insurance benefits cheque in their pocket.
Furthermore, we are going to decide whether we will continue this action to prevent future Government discrimination again retirees so there will not be two classes of workers in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) has just acknowledged that the early retirees of 1985 had a legitimate grievance. I am proud of this decision, all the more so because from day one I have been speaking on behalf of the Abitibi early retirees. In a press release dated May 20, 1986,1 stated:
Given the commitments made by their employers and the recommendations of the federal Government, justice will prevail for the Abitibi early retirees of 1985. Those who opted for retirement have since had their benefits reduced or cut off.
Since the state has chosen not to honour its contract with them, they can appeal this decision.
Mr. Speaker, I was elected to defend the interests of the people, and this is not the first time I fight for the well-being of elderly people in Abitibi. I appreciate the commendable job done by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Like an excellent CEGEP teacher, he has corrected the Government's essay.

subtopic: JOBS NEEDED BY FORESTRY GRADUATES
JOBS NEEDED BY FORESTRY GRADUATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 10 the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) said:
I'm particularly aware of our country's need for well educated foresters who will contribute invaluably to the continued prosperity of our number one industry.
If the Minister truly wants to see more professional foresters in Canada, he should act now to provide jobs for those foresters who are already trained.
A study of recent forestry graduates from UBC shows how Canada wastes the training and talents of these young people. Of 290 graduates between 1983 and 1986, only 141, or 48.6 per cent, have been able to find jobs as forestry professionals. Twenty-one per cent are still unemployed.
Three years ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised to create a separate Department of Forestry. He has not kept that promise. Both our forests and our foresters suffer from this failure to keep his word.
March 19, 1987

maintopic: VOLUNTEER GROUP'S EFFORTS TO SECURE DEPORTATION OF LANDED IMMIGRANTS CONVICTED OF CRIMINAL ACTIVITIES
VOLUNTEER GROUP'S EFFORTS TO SECURE DEPORTATION OF LANDED IMMIGRANTS CONVICTED OF CRIMINAL ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in this House today to draw attention to an issue of great importance to all Canadians. There is a group of concerned citizens in British Columbia who, under the leadership and motivation of Mrs. Christine Mellin, are giving tirelessly of their time and energy to ensure that the safety of all Canadians is maintained. Their cause is the immediate deportation of individuals who have landed immigrant status in Canada and who have been convicted of criminal activities.
I am proud of these people's selfless efforts on behalf of all Canadians and I would like to reassure them that we, as a Government, recognize the serious nature of this issue. Given the excellent work of the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) in protecting the rights of Canadians through recent changes to immigration policies, I am sure that he will give serious attention to the concerns of those I am representing here today. Evidence of their commitment is demonstrated by the more than 4,000 signatures on this petition that I hold in my hand.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE
REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Canada's agricultural crisis grows worse every day. The total farm debt in Canada in 1985 amounted to $21.6 billion. One year later, at the end of 1986, it had climbed to $22.5 billion and is still rising. In Ontario, Canada's most prosperous province, my province, the farm debt stands at $5.2 billion, Mr. Speaker. It is interesting to note that farmers owe ever more to the Farm Credit Corporation and that 22.2 per cent of payments are late. Mr. Speaker, I might point out that in 1982, the worst recession year, 410 farm bankruptcies were recorded in Canada. In 1986, with a Conservative Government which claims to have done so much for the agricultural community, the number of farm bankruptcies went up to 440. The situation is intolerable and I insist that the Conservative Government come to the assistance of Canadian agricultural producers.

subtopic: REDUCTION IN BANK RATE-CREDIT CARD COMPANIES' HIGH INTEREST CHARGES
REDUCTION IN BANK RATE-CREDIT CARD COMPANIES' HIGH INTEREST CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bank rate has plunged again. It has just been announced that it has dropped to a rate of 7.14 per cent. That is one reason the press can say that foreign investors just love Canada. It is a good place to do business again.
We must also be aware that the spread between the bank rate and the prime rate is now wider than it was last week. The challenge to the banks and lending institutions is to bring that prime rate down so it can benefit business people and consumers still more, and particularly credit card users.
The credit card rate is the same as it was when the prime rate was over 20 points. One must ask if the bank rate has to come down to nothing before credit card consumers will benefit.

subtopic: SITUATION OF CHILEANS IN BUENOS AIRES
SITUATION OF CHILEANS IN BUENOS AIRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 85 Chileans barred from Canada by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) are trapped in Buenos Aires. They cannot come to Canada and dare not return to Chile. They report recognizing Chilean secret police menacing them on the streets of Buenos Aires. After exhausting their money and the church aid available, they have slept in a park for two nights and live on the streets. They are drinking the nonpotable water available there but are lacking money for food. Some of these people are children under the age of two.
The Canadian charge d'affaires is quoted by The Globe and Mail as saying: "If they've been sleeping in the streets, it's because they've chosen to do so". What a disgrace to Canada's foreign service. She sounds like a direct descendant of Marie "Let-Them-Eat-Cake" Antoinette. Ms. Herrera of the UNHCR sounds more realistic. She has said: "You only have to talk to them to know they are destroyed, that they are afraid to return". What is the Minister's problem with Chileans? Is none too many?
March 19, 1987

subtopic: UNITED STATES COMMITMENT
UNITED STATES COMMITMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada and especially the Prime Minister have finally been successful in their efforts to convince the United States to join in the fight against acid rain. Yesterday, in Washington, the American President announced that his country would spend $5 billion to fight acid rain.
Mr. Speaker, over the past year our Government has often severely blamed the United States for their inaction in this matter and the announcement made yesterday in Washington is definitely a major step in the right direction. I feel it is important to remind the House that the commitment made yesterday by the American President is fully consistent with the main recommendation in the Lewis-Davis report made public in January 1986.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians can rest assured that the Prime Minister of Canada will strongly protect their interests in this matter to provide them with the quality of life they rightfully deserve.

subtopic: EFFECT OF LUMBER EXPORT TAX ON NORTHERN ONTARIO SAWMILL
EFFECT OF LUMBER EXPORT TAX ON NORTHERN ONTARIO SAWMILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I bring to the attention of the House and most particularly the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) a further effect of her so-called softwood lumber deal with the United States. Mr. Jack Lavallet, President of Kimberly-Clark Canada Limited, announced on Tuesday that the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber has had a negative impact on sawmill profitability. Consequently, his company has announced a shut-down of the Longlac sawmill in northern Ontario effective May 15 this year. This will result in a total loss of over 100 jobs. It is further proof of how the Government bungled the entire softwood lumber issue with the United States administration.
The Government was tested and it has been found wanting, and tragically so. I call upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote) immediately to take what steps they can to repair the damage done by their colleague, the Minister for International Trade.

maintopic: IMPORTANCE OF TRADE TO ECONOMY OF NORTHERN ONTARIO
IMPORTANCE OF TRADE TO ECONOMY OF NORTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear yesterday the comments of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) about the forestry sector of northern Ontario, especially after his Party spoke out against the Government's trade initiatives. That really showed how misinformed his Party is about the North. The facts are that seven out of 10 jobs in northern Ontario depend directly on trade. Some 200,000 people are employed in the mining sector and over 70,000 in the forestry sector. Canadian exports last year included over $19 billion worth of metals and $16 billion worth of wood and paper.
On average each $1 billion in exports leads to the creation of 15,000 jobs. A trade agreement with the U.S. will provide even more employment opportunities which are so important to our economy. The Conservative Government will meet the challenge of trade negotiations with the U.S. and further the vision of Canada. The Conservative Party has always been the Party of vision. It is our heritage and our obligation. Sir John A. Macdonald moulded it and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) of today will enhance it.

subtopic: HOUSING CONDITIONS ON RESERVES
HOUSING CONDITIONS ON RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak about something which affects not only my riding but those right across the country, that is, the condition of native housing. For many years native people, especially treaty Indians, have suffered from a deplorable housing situation. We have not had for a number of years any special effort by any Government at the federal level to come to grips with the problem. This year's Budget and Estimates do not provide money to help solve the problem.
I find it deplorable to walk into native housing in this country and find holes in floors, broken-down ceilings, and doors that do not close. It is deplorable that the Government is not coming to grips with the problem. I call upon the Government to develop a national strategy for native housing and announce it soon. There should be a five or six-year program to make sure we get rid of the backlog. There is no way native students will receive adequate education or live in a healthy environment unless the Government commits itself to such a program.

March 19, 1987
Oral Questions HUMAN RIGHTS

Mr. Speaker, Dobroslav Paraga is a young Yugoslavian who protested the human rights problem in that country. For that protest he was arrested and jailed for five years. When released he protested the torture inflicted on him by the state. As a result of that protest he was again arrested and prosecuted. It was only because of the excellent lawyer he had and because of ill health that the prosecution was temporarily stayed. I call on the Government of Yugoslavia to respect human rights as all Governments should respect human rights.

subtopic: AUTOMOBILES-USE OF REAR SEAT THREE POINT SAFETY BELTS
AUTOMOBILES-USE OF REAR SEAT THREE POINT SAFETY BELTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again today I want to put on the record a letter 1 received from Dr. Acker, President of the Medical Society of Nova Scotia. The letter deals with the need for three point safety belts for rear seat passengers. The letter reads:
Congratulations and thank you for your comments to the House February 11, 1987 concerning the need for increased safety measures for rear seat passengers. Your observations about the added safety provided by three point safety belts are quite correct.
The Medical Society raised this question a year ago. We pointed to the concern, noted that a mere handful of imported cars use the three point harness and reminded government of its commitment to car safety. Regrettably, no action has been taken by any government in Canada.
We have come a long way in vehicle safety, and we urge government to take the next logical step. We already require seat belts in our cars, let's require that those seat belts be the most effective.
Again, thanks for bringing this important matter before the House. Hoping your remarks will lead to action-

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It is becoming evident that the Government's acid rain strategy has failed so miserably-

speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext:
-that even getting President Reagan to live up to a year-old commitment is considered by the Prime Minister to be a very significant movement. We are now locked in a five-year research and demonstration program which will not benefit our dying lakes, forests, and eco-systems because there
is no commitment to cut acid rain entering Canada. As Michael Perley of the Canadian Coalition on Acid Rain put it, "clean coal technology isn't the solution to the problem . . . Emission reduction is the key".

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what we will do at the summit is continue the results of yesterday which constitute a very significant step forward in the fight against acid rain. We will continue that. Surely anyone who cares about the environment and understands anything about the devastating impact of acid rain on the environment, and appreciates the total absence of activity in regard thereto over the last 20 years, will celebrate yesterday's events but recognize that we have a long way to go. speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-44, an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal PostSecondary Education and Health Contributions Act, 1977, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before we broke for dinner today, I was indicating why I supported Bill C-44, the equalization payment Bill. I would like to recap my remarks and, in the 10 minutes I have left, highlight some of the reasons for my support of Bill C-44.
First, equalization payments for this year and next are increasing. Members of the Opposition have tried to imply that the equalization payments will not increase and I would like to put on record that in 1987-88, equalization payments for the provinces that receive them will be increasing from $5.3 billion to $5.6 billion and in 1988-89 they will increase to $5.9 billion. That is an increase of well over 5 per cent per year and it is in addition to the forgiveness of the over-payment which will amount to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $270 million.
The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) indicated earlier in his debate that the net forgiveness clause in the Bill would interfere with and cancel out the technical increases, but that is not correct. I do not know if the Hon. Member misunderstood the Bill or if he was trying to mislead the House, but there is no way to connect the net forgiveness in the over-payment with the technical changes. The technical changes are for future years while the forgiveness in the overpayment is for the past two years.
The Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) as well as the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides implied that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had indicated that the technical changes would be handled in one year. I would like to remind Hon. Members that the Minister of Finance indicated very clearly on December 17 in the House of Commons, in response to a question put by the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), the following:
Mr. Speaker, this proposal was made by officials of the provincial and federal Governments. The offer did not come from the federal Government. I told the provinces yesterday and last Friday that the federal Government could not possibly accept the one-year proposal. We were agreeable to an increase over two years, and that is what our Government has decided. This is in addition to the increase from 4 to 6 per cent in the annual increment for the equalization program.
The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides indicated, I believe, that there would be a $400 million loss in the major transfer payments. Again, that is incorrect. I would like to make it very clear to the House and to Canadians that the major federal transfers which are made up of the equalization
payments, the EPF and the Canada Assistance payments totalled $25,887 billion in 1986-87. The major federal transfers will be increased in the coming year to $27,328 billion, for a total increase to all the provinces of $1.44 billion. That is a lot of money. I like to say it is 27,328 millions of dollars in transfers to the provinces. In addition to that, another $2.5 billion will go to the provinces. I believe it is very clear that the payments are increasing.
I would like to comment on what this means to the province in which I live, Manitoba. The 1987 Manitoba Budget in Brief, under the heading "A Good Place to Live and Work", says that Manitoba's economic performance has been above average for Canada and is expected to lead other provinces again in 1987. The total transfer payments to Manitoba will represent $1,312 billion this year. Manitoba's Budget indicates that the budgetary expenditure for the Province of Manitoba this year will be $4,188 billion. The budgetary revenue, the amount of money collected through taxes and from the transfers from the federal Government, will represent $3,773, resulting in a net deficit budget requirement of $415 million. The $1,312 billion that the federal Government will be transferring to the province in the coming year compared to the $3,773 billion that will be collected means that over 35 cents of every dollar raised in Manitoba will be coming from federal transfer payments. At that point, the provincial Government must take some responsibility. If it wishes to spend on programs, many of which I support, then I believe it is also its responsibility to raise the revenues and not just get the money from the federal Government. As I mentioned earlier, there is only one federal taxpayer, there is only one provincial taxpayer and there is only one municipal taxpayer.
I believe Governments should be responsible. The federal Government has been responsible in trying to control the deficit. As the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankow-ski) just mentioned a few moments ago, the Bank of Canada interest rate has fallen to 7.14 per cent today. What does that mean to the provinces? Most of the provinces have accumulated debts on which they will be paying lower interest charges this year. Even the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) recognized the other day that the lower interest rate will be beneficial to the provinces.
W'hy is the interest rate lower? It is because the people of the world know that Canada is trying to control its debt. As a result, they have confidence in our dollar. The interest rate has gone down because of the confidence in the dollar. Inflation is down. This will benefit all the different levels of Government. I say that the different levels of Government must take some responsibility and I call upon them to be fair about this.
The equalization payments to Manitoba this year will be $441 million for 1986-87 and they will grow to $469 million in 1987-88. That represents roughly $435 per person and accounts for more than 10 per cent of the actual revenue collected in the province. That is unconditional money. There are no strings attached to it whatsoever. The province can do whatever it wants with that money.

As well, my province benefited from the estimate of the number of people in the province to the tune of another $15 million this year. Instead of being forgiven an overpayment, the province will receive an extra $15 million. When we add up the $1,312 billion the province will receive from the federal Government, it means in excess of $1,200 per person. I commend our Government for that. As I indicated earlier, this will account for approximately 35 per cent of the Manitoba Budget, not counting the money it has to borrow. This is a 6 per cent increase in a province which is one of the leaders in economic growth in Canada.
I know we all benefit from equalization payments. I know Manitoba benefits quite well. It is in our Constitution and I support it. We have to recognize the different regions of our country and the fact we should all have a certain quality of life regardless of where we live.

Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker) for straightening out the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau). That Hon. Member seems to be thoroughly confused about the national debt. I saw him on national television a couple of weeks ago misinforming and handing out false information to the Canadian people. He called this Government's Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) the king of deficits. I am sure he is a little confused. What he should have said was that it was the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) who was the architect of our national debt.
I will explain to him what happened and how we got into this ridiculous situation under successive Liberal Governments. In 1972, when the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra was the Minister of Finance, he inherited a surplus of $700 million. In 1975 he left and there was a deficit of almost $5 billion. That is referred to as the Turner formula. The Right Hon. Member introduced blank cheque government to this country, uncontrolled spending and the encouraging of empirebuilding. The Liberals did not even know how many Crown corporations they had. That formula was carried on by Macdonald, MacEachen, Chretien and all the rest. That Turner blank cheque formula was stopped in 1984. If we had not taken control of expenditures the deficit would be $42 billion this year. We have reduced it by $10 billion.
It is very easy to be a Liberal or a New Democrat. They have one theory and one philosophy. You solve all problems by spending more money. About 90 per cent of the questions they

While there is other tax revenue, 80 cents out of every dollar in federal income tax goes to pay the interest on the outstanding debt and that is why we must get control of the deficit, as my hon. colleague indicated.

Member explain his comment about a need for reduced deficits in the provinces when the federal Government is not doing its share in meeting the needs of those provinces?

Madam Speaker, the major federal transfers have increased, not decreased as the Hon Member has indicated. They will increase in excess of 5 per cent per year.

In Manitoba, the EPF payment in 1985-86 was $610 billion, in 1986-87 it will be $648 billion, and in 1987-88 it will be $681 billion. It increases quite substantially every year, in excess of some 6 per cent per year.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on a Bill that concerns equalization payments and cash transfers to the provinces. Madam Speaker, being a Quebecer yourself, you will understand my reaction. Today's poll shows that 50 per cent would have voted for the Liberals and 17 per cent for the Conservatives. It is just as well the polling firm did not include the Rhinoceros Party in its questionnaire, because the Conservatives would have come fourth with 7 per cent, while the Rhinoceros Party would have had 10 per cent. And when you watch the Government and the Prime Minister, I think they are just as entertaining as the Rhinos.
On the subject of equalization payments, Mr. Gerard D. Levesque, the Quebec Minister of Finance, and the Hon. Robert Bourassa, the Premier of Quebec and a man I hold in high esteem, who has made his mark and has shown a great deal of courage, both these gentlemen are demanding the province's fair share. We are not asking for sympathy. We are not asking for charity. We are asking for our fair share.
At this very moment, the Government of Quebec is claiming $91 million it is owed by the federal Government.
I have here a document dated April 2, 1985. Of course the House is well aware Premier Bourassa is a Member of the Liberal Party. For Quebec, however, it is not a matter of politics, it is a matter of justice. The document in question was signed by Mr. Yves Duhaime, then Minister of Finance in the Parti Quebecois Government, and like Premier Bourassa and Quebec Minister of Finance, Mr. Gerard D. Levesque, he was claiming reimbursement of money owed and felt that the way Quebecers were being treated by this Conservative Government was entirely unfair and unacceptable. At the time, they were claiming $81 million, as a result of the inaction and incompetence of this Government, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister. And today, Quebec is still lagging behind.
What are the consequences of this lack of cash transfers from the federal Government to Quebecers? It has meant a loss of billions of dollars for secondary education, health insurance and hospital insurance programs. Who is affected by this situation? If it were just a quarrel or a conflict between the Quebec Minister of Finance and the Minister of Finance in Ottawa, a personality conflict, for instance, his limousine is bigger than mine or one Minister travels more than the other, I wouldn't even bother. However, the consequences are borne by ordinary citizens. Less money for post-secondary education will penalize our sons and daughters. There will be less money to educate our children. More poor families will have to let
March 19, 1987

their children join the labour market instead of finishing school.
As for the cutbacks in health care, they affect our families, our children, and the entire population of Quebec, especially as far as health care and hospital services are concerned in regions such as Bellechasse and the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean, where it is more difficult to find doctors and adequate services such as exist in the major centres like Montreal and Quebec City, where the people are well taken care of and where there are full services in community centres, as well as accommodations and emergency home services.
The media often tell us about the overcrowding in the emergency rooms of our hospitals. The Quebec Minister of Elealth and Welfare, Mrs. Lavoie-Roux, is finding it very difficult to solve this problem, even though everyone in Quebec would like to do so, whether they are Pequistes, Liberals or something else, but whenever they sit down at a table to try to find an answer, someone very, very smart in Ottawa says that he will cut off their funds. This reminds me of what happened yesterday. Since I am speaking about senior citizens and early retirement... I can see Conservative Members from Quebec, who are always ready to applaud anything that the Minister says. They act like clowns, they always smile and say that everything is perfect. As for me, I have worked on three rather important issues, and in the case of senior citizens who demanded justice once for six weeks and then for 14 months, the Government finally had to admit that a mistake had been made. Then how come with old age security pension indexing, senior citizens had to demonstrate on Parliament Hill. Mrs. Denis even had to address the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) sharply and Members of the Opposition had to complain for weeks before the Government admitted it was wrong?
In the field of health, the same thing happened with the 10 percent tax on medecine. Together with Members of the Opposition, people suffering from diabetes, cardio-vascular and respiratory diseases had to constantly pressure the Government for four or five months to bring the Prime Minister and the Cabinet to the realization that they had made a mistake. Tory Members never rise in the House to protect the interests of these people.
Again, yesterday, the 35,000 early retirees in Canada, including 13,000 in Quebec, have succeeded and forced the Minister of Employment and Immigration for the first time and the Prime Minister for the third time to admit that they had been wrong. But why is it that no Tory Member in the House, whether representing Quebec, Alberta, Ontario, Atlantic or Western Canada, has ever managed to convince the Prime Minister by telling him: My dear Prime Minister, you are dead wrong.
For instance, let us look at matters strictly of interest to Quebec. The aerospace centre for instance. There again, Quebec is about to be hoodwinked. The same thing in the case

of equalization payments, tax point transfers, post-secondary education, as well as health programs and hospitalization services.
Let us take for instance the famous promise concerning the Banking Centre in Montreal. Everybody here knows that I am a Montrealer, beside being a Quebecer and a Canadian. I am a citizen of the Montreal-Sainte-Marie riding. The formal promise made by the Prime Miniser to Montrealers: the International Banking Centre will solve all your problems. In fact, what we got was a night counter, a night teller. The guy who lives far away would be able to make a deposit in Montreal at night. That is of no use; it is a joke. These are nothing but half-measures.
There are other Quebec programs, including equalization, which have been poorly put together including the cleaning up of the St. Lawrence River polluted water which is again in the news. Mr. Clift Lincoln, the Quebec Minister of Environment, is not asking for a hand out but something similar to what other provinces have already received, in order to help Quebec clean up the St. Lawrence River.
In view of the fact that this request came from Quebec, the federal response, as in the area of equalization, is no. Another similar issue-you know that over the past few months, a large number of refugees have come to the province of Quebec, to Montreal. Faced with this situation, Mrs. Robic, the Quebec Minister responsible for ethnic groups, turned to Ottawa and ever so gently asked for assistance, in view of this particular situation, to help Quebec foot the bill. Again, because it was a Quebec request, the answer was no.
There were also requests for funds to help Montreal-East and the shipyards. Quebec shipyards still have a major role to play and used to be a job creation industry. Let us look at the Lauzon shipyards near Quebec City. In four instances, six months ago, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion promised those people that 1,000 workers would be hired to work there. There are now approximately ten workers in the yards, and the 1,000 others who expected to get jobs on the construction of the Caribou II have just been told that this may have to wait until next October. So there is another delay.
At the Sorel shipyards, which have quite a reputation, the Marine Industries yards, there again 200 layoffs are expected within the next two months. The only remaining work involves contracts that were awarded by the previous Liberal Government.
And at the Versatile Vickers yards, well, two weeks from now the naval section in Montreal will be shut down.
There you have 5,000 Quebec workers who have been demonstrating for the past year and a half. All the employees of all the companies have been here on Parliament Hill. They have met with the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine), the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, with Members from the entire Quebec region. On each occasion there were promises, but again not one darn job has yet been created.

The same thing goes for Sorel. The former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote) told on Parliament Hill: "That is settled. Don't worry, fellows, I am looking after that." He has looked after himself, and is no longer a minister.
Same thing in Montreal. There was the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret)-when the Montreal East end issue came up, there were five Ministers dealing with it, five Ministers on that committee: The President of the Treasury Board, the former Minister of Environment, the now Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) and the former Minister of State for Small Businesses. Two Ministers had to resign from that committee. They were never replaced. And not a single job has yet been created in Montreal East end.
If the Gulf refinery is in operation, it is thanks to a Minister in Quebec, the Minister of Energy, Mr. Ciaccia, who decided to roll up his sleeves. Now, 250 employees are working there. It is not because of the Hon. Member for Montreal-Mercier (Mrs. Jacques), the Hon. Member for Gamelin (Mr. Gravel), nor the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (Mr. Desrosiers). It is simply because people in Montreal East end, whether PQ, Liberals, members of the Civic Party, of the RCM, representatives of all labour federations, union and nonunion people, they all joined in. The only ones who bickered among themselves in public were Conservative Members.
What about the Matane paper mill, the Desbiens paper mill, potato producers? We see another injustice there. Even the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Prime Minister were sent in to open the Matane paper mill. There was a big party. After the party, pictures were taken. Two weeks later they were announcing: No, no go! Nothing has been started yet. Words again! That is all our national camera kid can do, give a small handshake. I will settle all that. You may be sure that at the present rate, you will get nothing.
Let us look at what is going on in the footwear industry or better still with the former Melchers employees. The matter was thought to be solved. They were in to meet me as recently as two months ago asking me to intervene because they were unable to meet their Member who is a minister of the Crown, the Hon. Member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Lanaudiere (Mr. de Cotret).
Now, the footwear industry. In the past, the Quebec caucus had always stood against the officials and even the Prime Minister who was opposed to quotas, to protect the footwear industry. What did the Quebec Tory Members do? Niet. Nothing. Footwear quotas were removed. They all applauded because the then Minister said in his speech: "No problem!" What is going on today? One year later, 4,000 jobs have been lost. Industries have been affected not only in the Montreal area but also in Trois Rivieres, and Shawinigan where large manufactures were providing jobs which fostered regional economy.
I see that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) is here and this reminds me of another project. There was the preretirement plan in designated sectors or for the so-called designated industries and I will explain, Madam Speaker. The footwear industry as well as the textile and clothing industries had a program in designated districts such as the Thetford and Sorel areas as well as in other areas which could also make use of it. Under that program, if the footwear industry as a result of modernization or changes had to dismiss some of its employees, workers aged 55 years or over were eligible to what was called preretirement under the unemployment insurance scheme which allowed those workers who had not found jobs in their areas to draw unemployment insurance benefits up to their age of retirement. It is an vital program in remote areas. The Government, the Minister of Finance announced a new adjustment program for workers. And all of a sudden, the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of Labour terminated the existing program which gave early retirees the right to collect unemployment insurance benefits. In their announcements, they said: We are going to negotiate a new adjustment program for workers with the provinces, and the program will be retroactive. This was six months ago, and nothing has been done yet. The Minister of Labour is there, but nothing has been done. If a plant or a factory closes tomorrow, no one will be entitled to the safeguards of this program. This is another instance where the federal Government wanted to save on unemployment insurance benefits. It wanted to give less than welfare, and it was asking the provinces to make up the difference. And that is why the Minister of Labour cannot rise in the House and say: Mr. Malepart or the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie is wrong, we have an excellent program. There is no program. So far there has been no progress whatsoever. And not a single Conservative Member has raised this point. I have the impression they didn't know and that it is definitely news to them. I only hope that at least the Minister of Labour, a good Quebecer, realizes things are not going according to plan and that although so far he has been left in peace, this may be the next issue to get a going over. I advise him not to follow the example of his other colleagues and to settle before he is forced to. I think we have here a series of issues that clearly show . . . It is not surprising why only 17 per cent of the people of Quebec trust the Conservatives and that between 71 and 76 per cent do not trust the Prime Minister and the Conservative Government. It is all quite simple. The evidence is there and these are the people speaking. These are the people who elected this Government and who are now prepared to throw them out tomorrow. I have the impression that the longer they postpone the election, the fewer Conservative Members they will have left. They will be an endangered species!
Madam Speaker, since I have only one minute left, I want to urge Members from Quebec to sit up and take notice! I think it is high time somebody rose in the House and told the Minister ... In fact, to be honest, two of them did. The Hon.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Bill C-44 is a very serious piece of legislation, since it will cut equalization payments to the province of Quebec by about $71 million and payments to the province of Manitoba by a fairly substantial amount. In fact, it is in line with this Government's policy to cut the growth of equalization payments and tax transfers to the provinces by billions of dollars, which will increase disparities among the provinces.
Madam Speaker, I must say I am disappointed in the remarks just made by the Parliamentary Secretary, who looks at the fight against the deficit as his Government's sole priority, without any consideration for an employment situation that remains urgent in many of our provinces. In seven provinces, the unemployment rate is still higher than it was in 1981-82 during the recession. I am also disappointed in the attitude taken by the Official Opposition, which is trying to raise all kinds of points of order instead of getting on with the debate on this very important matter.
On that side they are not being serious enough about this, while the Government side is making the fight against the deficit its sole priority, without any consideration for the impact on Canadian men and women of the regional disparities existing today in this country. Madam Speaker, perhaps this explains why today in the Province of Quebec, for instance, the polls indicate that the Conservatives have fallen to the lowest level ever, 17 per cent, at the same time as the New Democratic Party rose to 34 per cent in polls throughout the country and 34 per cent as well in the Province of Quebec, the highest level we have ever reached since World War II.
Madam Speaker, I want to remind my friends in all Parties how this happened in history. During World War II the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, which preceded the New Democratic Party, brought every kind of pressure to bear on
March 19, 1987

the then Liberal Government to promote a social policy, a welfare policy, a full employment policy after the war. All Canadians had been disillusioned by the great depression. They wanted to make sure that, once the war was over, our country would be looking forward to a much more promising future than what they had lived through in the 1930s. Sure enough, they turned to the New Democratic Party because throughout World War II the CCF had been the only Party to claim that governments must serve the people, not major financial interests, not major companies, not the Canadian elite only.
Well, Madam Speaker, the pressure exerted by the CCF was so effective that, although we had only a handful of Members in the House of Commoms at that time, Canadian public opinion expressed itself through polls and all sorts of indications, to the point where they prompted the Government of former Prime Minister Mackenzie King to come up with a full employment policy.
The Liberal Government responded to the general wish for a Government which would show some concern for the needs of the people. For instance, the family allowance program was introduced, and so were some of the major social programs which now provide some support for all Canadians. It was only three years after the Second World War that the hospital insurance program came into being, and it too was due to the leadership shown by the CCF in Saskatchewan.
I am recalling these historical events, Madam Speaker, to reply to the Parliamentary Secretary who says, just like the Government did in 1983, that the priorities of the Canadian population, as expressed in the polls and as stated by the New Democratic Party, are of no interest whatsoever to the Conservative Government. Instead of wanting to follow the example of the former Liberal Government in the forties, instead of wanting to change the policies of the Government to develop a full employment policy, a policy to eliminate regional disparities among the provinces, a policy to maintain social programs, the Parliamentary Secretary is saying that he supports the policy of fighting the deficit and doing nothing to meet the other needs of Canadians. Obviously, the deficit is important. Everyone knows it, but unemployment is also important, as is the fight against regional disparities. It is in this context, Madam Speaker, that I want to make some comments on Bill C-44.
I would like to remind all my friends in the House of Commons and all Canadians who are watching this debate that, with this Bill, the Government is imposing a solution after failing in all its efforts to achieve a consensus among the provinces. There were indeed many meetings. That there was no agreement with the provinces is mostly due to the fact that the Government wanted to save money at their expense. Finally, this solution had to be forced on them.
This Bill brings about a technical change to the provincial equalization program. It will provide $175 million a year to the provinces and the Minister of Finance has promised that this will apply for one year.

But after having made all those promises on television, in public, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) changed his views, and now he will be putting that change in place over a two year period.
Madam Speaker, in view of the announcement made the other day by the Minister and in Bill C-44, I accept that they will not require a refund of overpayments made to provinces and that were discovered following the 1985 census. This means Quebec will not have to repay certain monies received under the equalization program without being entitled to them because its population had been over-estimated but that now have to be adjusted. But in the same breath, the Government insists that Quebec waive its claim to certain adjustments in the order of $100 million for fiscal year 1985-86, and I think for 1986-87.
It is also true, Madam Speaker, that in Quebec the other technical changes that are very important have to do with the payment checking program for established program funding and equalization payments. There seems to be very little time allowed for checking the figures, to make sure they are accurate. If there are indeed errors, the Canadian Government refuses to change its calculations. Quebec would like to be allowed a three to six months period after the final evaluation, in order that the provinces may check the figures. The technical change has not yet been made, but hopefully, after the representations made before the committee, that technical change can be made.
Madam Speaker, I note particularly the fact that the equalization scheme pursued by the Government is at odds with the commitments entrenched in the Constitution that equalization must be used to remove disparities between provinces and ensure that each province can provide comparable levels of public services at comparable levels of taxation.
Madam Speaker, I see in the Estimates for 1987-1988 an increase of only 2 per cent in the equalization payments and other payments with regard to that area. However, Madam Speaker, here are the figures as they appear in the Estimates, Part I, relating to government expenditures: it is indicated in the table, on page 40, that the fiscal transfer payments will increase from $5,768 billions in the 1986-1987 Main Estimates to $5.9 billions in 1987-1988. The difference is $134 millions or 2.3 per cent. That is all. Now, Madam Speaker, we have just heard someone describing the situation prevailing in Saskatchewan. We are familiar with the difficult situation in Alberta due to the decrease in oil prices and the problems with that industry. One wonders whether a mere 2.3 per cent increase in equalization payments will be enough to make up for increasing disparities in our country, a country where the unemployment rate in southern Ontario is down to 5 per cent and even to 4 per cent in some areas like Toronto, Kitchener and Waterloo, while it stays higher in seven other provinces, an unemployment rate like the one that prevailed during the 1981-82 recession. Will such a small increase be enough? I do not think it will.

March 19, 1987
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
I would also like to quote, Madam Speaker, from the French version of the summary of the Government Expenditure Plan regarding fiscal transfer payments: Fiscal transfer payments include equalization payments, subsidies under the Constitution Acts, Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer and Reciprocal Taxation. Equalization payments, accounting for some 95 per cent of these transfers, are unconditional payments to provinces to raise, to some standard level, the per capita revenue-raising capacity of lower-income provinces, in order that they can provide their residents with reasonable levels of public services at reasonable levels of taxation. The standard is determined by the average fiscal capacity of the five provinces of British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec.
In fact, what the Government says is that he wants to raise, to some standard level, the revenue-raising capacity of the provinces, in order that they can provide their residents with reasonable levels of public services at reasonable levels of taxation. Now, I would like to quote Section 36(2) of the Constitution Act, 1981 according to which Parliament and the government of Canada are committed to the principle of making equalization payments to ensure that provincial government have sufficient revenues to provide reasonably comparable levels of public services at reasonably comparable levels of taxation. There is no double standard to the Constitution; it is a comparable standard for everybody.
When a province like Newfoundland levies a sales tax of 11 or 12 per cent while in Ontario this same tax is only 7 per cent, would you say they are comparable? I would say no. If differences of income tax rates are as high as 40 percent from one province to another, can we say that personal incomes tax rates are comparable in Canada? Again, I say they are not.
If the provincial Minister of Finance suggests that Newfoundland is on the verge of bankrupcy because of income tax problems, can we, in all fairness, compare the situation of his province to that of Ontario where the liberal government has just received actually a heavenly gift of one billion dollars which has been already spent on gifts, new expenditures, new programs and so on? The premier of Ontario has just been visiting in Ottawa where he announced a $10 million grant to the Cardiology Research Centre at the Civic Hospital in my riding. It is a welcome announcement indeed but could the premier of Newfoundland do the same? The answer is no because Newfoundland does not have the same fiscal capacity as Ontario. Why is the commitment made in our Constitution apparently ignored by this government in its description of the fiscal transfer payment program for the 1987-88 fiscal year? Indeed, instead of providing public services at a roughly comparable level of quality the government now changes that commitment so that that level of quality be set according to an established standard. If I may, this is what they say in English and I quote:

Equalization payments-are unconditional payments to provinces to raise, to
some standard level, the per capita revenue-raising capacity of lower-income
provinces, in order that they can provide their residents with reasonable levels
of public services at reasonable levels of taxation.
Now, Madam Speaker, does that mean reasonable as compared with Bangladesh, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) said a while ago, or as compared with all other Canadian jurisdictions? That is the question we must ask ourselves. And the Government would indeed answer that "reasonable" means as compared with England, perhaps with France, perhaps with underdeveloped countries, but certainly not with all the other provinces.
In fact, the Conservative Government, in power now for only two and a half years, fails to honour an undertaking that all three political Parties had solemnly taken during the Constitutional debate of 1981 and 1982.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I wish to say that we recognize, in our Party, how difficult it is to achieve full employment. I have just read this morning's editorial in The Globe and Mail, which states very clearly the economic performance of the Manitoba Government, showing how the NDP Government has reduced the unemployment rate and brought the growing rate of the economy to be the highest projected of all provinces for the fiscal year 87-88. I could always refer to the economic record of the New Democratic Governement in the Yukon Territory. About a year or a year and a half ago, they inherited a situation with an unemployment rate close to 20 per cent. Within a year, they reduced this rate by half. These, Madam Speaker, are the results of a real policy of full employment.
Last weekend, Madam Speaker, the NPD held its convention. I know that many Quebec voters watched us since it was held in Montreal for the first time. Yes, a great many of them did. I say to the Parliamentary Secretary-many of his constituents voted NDP because of our efforts in the province of Quebec.

I already asked the question: How is it that according to Statistics Canada figures for the period going from January 1986 to January 1987, on the 137,000 new jobs created in Canada, only 5,000 were to be found in nine provinces while the 132,000 others went to Ontario? Is this the kind of fairness the Government is looking for? How can Quebec and the other provinces overcome the problem of disparities? How will they find enough tax revenues to pay for all the necessary programs and ensure their economic development if the jobs created are all concentrated in one province only, namely the Southern part of Ontario? This is the question. The Finance Minister often tells us that he is committed to achieve fairness among provinces and all the rest. But people won't judge only by his words but also by the facts. And when I look at the performance of this Government, I see that the bulk of the economic growth taking place at the present time in the country is concentrated in Southern Ontario. Surely this development is to be welcomed but that doesn't compensate for the fact that the recession continues in the rest of the country. This is unacceptable.
