subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867-1982-REFORM
speechtext:
I thank my colleagues. My point is that whether or not one agrees with the politics of particular governments, since Confederation there have only been two Parties in the upper House, the Liberals and Conservatives. The numbers of Liberals or Conservatives depended upon the tenure of the Government in power.
Until recently there were three Governments-the Parti Quebecois in Quebec, the New Democratic Party in Manitoba, and the Social Credit Party in British Columbia-which at no time had a political say in the affairs of the Government of Canada. Whether or not one agrees with their politics, they were refused the right to have spokesmen in the upper House of Canada.
As part of my concept of the upper House, I want to deal with how the Senate would actually function. I state in my motion that where a Bill is not adopted by the Senate within ten sitting days after its receipt from the House of Commons, the Senate may require that the Bill be submitted to a joint conference committee of the two Chambers. Today, a Bill that is passed by the House of Commons will go to the Senate where it may sit interminably. Conversely, a Bill originating in the Senate may come to the House of Commons and sit here interminably. There has not been an effective refusal of a Commons Bill in the Senate for many years, and the reverse is true.
It seems to me that if both Houses are to do their job they should be in a position to seriously criticize and amend either's proposed legislation. However, there must be a provision that if a Bill goes to the Senate and sits there for a specific time and is not dealt with, it can come back to the House for final passage. As well, the reverse must be true.
If a Bill is sent back from one House to the other, there should be a joint conference committee of the two Chambers, made up of senior members who would, in their wisdom and experience, deal with the Bill and send it back to both Houses to either be passed after that joint consideration or left to die. In areas where such a procedure works, it is very rare that a Bill is allowed to die. There may be some changes but eventually the Bills are passed.
In conclusion, I have proposed a suggestion for a Senate. I do not favour abolishing the Senate because I believe it protects Canadians in many ways. I like the idea of a Senate that is more representative of the regions but I oppose the suggestion of an elected Senate. I believe the original thought of our forefathers in having the Senate above elections is worth
March 19, 1987

while and my suggestion to the House is that there are ways of appointing Senators, providing there are rules that makes it work to the benefit of all Canadians.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867-1982-REFORM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to address this resolution this afternoon, essentially on my own. I am speaking from the Liberal side of the House and I do sit in the front benches. I am briefed and committed to the policy resolutions of our Party which I intend to share with the House, and I am committed to the views of our leader. However, I want to give some personal reactions because I believe I can make as good a contribution to the debate in that way.
The fundamental problem with the Senate, as I see it, is a problem of legitimacy. The Senate has a tremendous power that is legally and constitutionally the equivalent of the power we have in this Chamber.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867-1982-REFORM
speechtext: Ostensible.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867-1982-REFORM
speechtext:
My friend, the mover of the motion, is saying that the power is ostensible. The power is real. The power is constitutionally valid. No legislation in Canada can be enacted unless the other place deals with it and adopts it. Therefore, the power is real, but the legitimacy is missing because Canadians know and Senators know, and many of them have said that it would be unacceptable for the Senators to use power in the same way that we do so proudly and defensively in this place.
We make decisions, we speak for the Canadian people, and we have the credentials to prove it. Our membership in the House is established in such a way that we represent the people of Canada and I suggest that we would find it difficult to accept the negation of our will by the other place, even though it is proper to do that constitutionally.
That creates a dilemma for them in the other place. I imagine they want to perform their function but the only way they can do so under the present set-up might cancel the work that was done in this House. There is something significantly wrong with the Senate and I believe it is its legitimacy.
I do not believe this resolution addresses fully the problem of legitimacy. The mover of the motion mentioned at the outset that he did not want to deal with the proportionate representation by Senators. I appreciate that he is choosing not to address that, but I suggest that it is an essential component of a Senate reform package.
I want to talk about that for a moment because otherwise there is not much point in trying to market some of the ideas dealt with in this resolution directly. The Senate needs reform along the lines proposed by our Party at its national convention, which is that Senators should come from each province in equal numbers. That may shock the Hon. Member opposite if he did not know that our Party passed that resolution. But it does state that the Liberal Party of Canada has committed itself to an elected Senate with equal representation from each province.
Senate Reform
This means that if Yukon, if it achieves provincial status, or little Prince Edward Island, will have the same strength in the other place as Ontario and Quebec. We are making this proposal to point out the need in this country for regions to feel that they have a voice here. This is particularly important in view of the behaviour of the present Government in relation to regional development or regional priorities. The Government committed itself to regional programs. It came to office and is awarding government contracts and business on a political basis. I only need remind Members about the decision on the CF-18.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867-1982-REFORM
speechtext: Relevance.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867-1982-REFORM
speechtext:
I think it is very relevant. I believe that people feel if they had an equal voice per province in the Senate that type of abuse could be stopped. They cannot look to the Senate to stop it now because it has a legitimacy problem. If the members of the Senate were chosen on an equal basis by the regions, as the Liberal Party recommends, I think people would look to the Senate. If there was a defense for what the Government was doing then the defense could be made in the Senate, chosen the way I have recommended.
When we look at the principle of representation in this House, which is "rep by pop", we have to ask ourselves why Prince Edward Island should have the same number of members as Ontario, and will it work. We think it should have, and we think it would work. Perhaps the best way in which I could demonstrate this is by using the example of the United States where Rhode Island has the same number of Senators as does California and New York. It does work. It would be an effective way of showing the Senate to Canadians as a place that has a legitimate right to intervene in our procedure. Canadians would accept its basis on that score.
I now wish to turn to the second point, which is whether Senators should be chosen on any basis other than on an election basis. Under the present system they are all chosen by the Prime Minister, by the Governor in Council. The recommendation in the resolution before us is that half of each province's delegation should be chosen as it is now and the other half should be chosen, in effect, by the provincial Government. Our resolution calls for direct election.
I want to try to convince the Hon. Member of the advantages of direct election. I heard his argument against it when he addressed the question. I am afraid that in the type of Senate he has proposed the temptation of a province with a desperate problem, with a perspective on national affairs, would be to send a delegated group to Ottawa knowing that they would be replaced from time to time as elections occur. This delegated group would be sent to Ottawa to speak for the perspective of the Government of the day governing that province. I can see a provincial Government using this forum to give some of its players a chance to strut their stuff on the national scene, to improve their credentials, perhaps for

March 19, 1987
Senate Reform
leadership of a party, or to improve their credentials for running for office in a riding which would be open in a future provincial election, or something of that nature. In other words, with this type of formula, especially with the reappointment provision, I can see Senators coming here under this procedure with a special agenda in mind.
One thing that can be said for the Senators who are chosen under our present system is that when they come here they tend to come for life. Of course, there have been one or two exceptions, but they tend to come for life. If they lose interest along the way and take an early retirement, while retaining their seat in the other place-retiring in the sense of their continuing contribution to public affairs-at least they do not have the other agenda which is: "Boy, as soon as the election comes along I'm running for a seat in Prince Edward Island", or a seat in Ontario.
1 would like to see Senators come here from their provinces in the national interest. I do not think this motion achieves that. I am worried that provincial appointees will not rise above a provincial perspective. I am worried that the knowledge that they will not be reappointed, or may not be reappointed, will cause them to think ahead about their next career. Nothing is more fair than having an election to choose a spokesperson for the people of the country. Therefore I prefer to see the direct election of Senators, which is what my Party recommends.
Finally, I wish to address one other aspect of the question concerning the legitimacy of the Senate. I do not think that there should be equal authority as between the two Chambers. I think that if we move to an elected Senate the dispersal of power, in the type of checks and balances system we have, would weaken the national government in a way that would be against the national interest. I think a reformed Senate should have less authority, even with elected Senators. They should have less authority than those who are elected to this place which chooses the Government and to which the Government is accountable. This idea is not part of my Party's resolution. It is my own thinking with respect to how we would fill in the blanks. So I would like to see them have some sort of suspensory authority by which they could hold up legislation for a while.
In that connection I would like to turn to the idea that 10 days or 15 days is enough, as this motion proposes, for the Senate to gather its points of view together, and, failing to do so, then have a conference. I do not think that is realistic. I think the suspensory period should be for 90 days or 120 days, or something of that nature. In any event, it should be longer than 10 days.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867-1982-REFORM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure today to participate in this debate on yet another scheme for Senate reform. We spend enough time in this Chamber gilding lilies, we are now apparently reduced to gilding weeds. I say that since the resolution before us essentially envisages an expansion of the existing powers which
the Senate now has, that is one thing members of my Party could not contemplate under any circumstances.
The previous speaker spoke of a Liberal policy resolution for an elected Senate. He went into some detail as to the virtues of such a scheme. In listening to him I think that each and every one of us was surely asking ourselves, and would ask him had we the opportunity, what possible significance a Liberal Party policy resolution-almost a contradiction in terms, as I am sure my hon. colleagues will note-could possibly have for the deliberations of this Chamber or, indeed, for the agenda of the country.
I think it was last week that we had a resolution before the Chamber that corresponded quite closely to a Liberal Party policy resolution that had been debated and voted on at that Party's convention last fall. If I recall correctly there were some 20-odd, perhaps close to 30, members of that Party who voted against the position of the Party as set out in the policy resolution. There were about four brave souls who saw fit to uphold the position in this Chamber that their Party had adopted in their policy convention. So much for the relevance of Liberal Party policy resolutions. After all, we are not here to discuss an elected Senate, which we can conveniently and perhaps with some pleasure dispose of as a viable contribution to Canada's constitutional debate at another time.
Essentially, what we are looking at is a resolution which, if it were to pass, would pit tradition and the Constitution against each other, even in a worse way than the Constitution has already been pitted against our most valued democratic traditions. This was the most unfortunate consequence of the 1982 constitutional entrenchment process. I say that because until we had the 1982 Constitution Act Canada's democratic traditions, which were inherited from the mother of Parliaments, Westminster, transplanted and grown ever more vigorous in the free and democratic soil of our country, stipulated a role for the Senate that was appropriate to the way in which the Senate is formed and the way in which it, if I can use the term ever so loosely, is regenerated. Up until 1982 it was clear to anyone who studied political science and to anyone who understood the democratic traditions of our country that the Senate did not have the power or the ability to impede or prevent the House of Commons from passing legislation. Of course, there would be those who will say that it is not the House of Commons, it is merely the Government of the day. Let them say that. For as I now sit on the opposition benches let me say that I will forever uphold the right of the Government, any Government, to legislate and to bring into law any project of legislation which it can persuade the majority in the House of Commons to pass.
In 1982 the Constitution was essentially silent on that lack of power with the Senate and some bold spirits, perhaps going against the democratic traditions of Canada, have argued that the Senate now in fact has the power to impede legislation. My hon. friend, the Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), stated
March 19, 1987

that the Senate was lacking legitimacy. It is now ever more lacking in legitimacy and was even before the last Liberal Government started its rampage of patronage appointments which contributed to its well-merited defeat in the last election.
I would even make the argument that the continued existence of the upper House is essentially un-Canadian because ever since Confederation in 1867 we in Canada, through the provincial legislatures, have followed a tradition of abolishing upper houses. Today we have reached the point where only one upper House remains, that being at the federal level. I, of course, would be glad to see that upper House abolished in the due course of time.
It seems that the resolution envisages something along the American model. I might point out that that which the Hon. Member for York Centre was proposing as a Liberal alternative was also modelled along the constitutional lines of the United States of America which has an equal number of Senators from each state. I ask all Members of this House and all Canadians to consider whether these imported models are relevant to the Canadian situation, or whether we as Canadians would not be much better advised, rather than striking out into uncharted waters and unknown territory, to continue the tradition which has been established at the provincial level and abolish this relic of history, the upper House, which has for so long haunted us and which now seems to have a very real danger of impeding the democratic will of the country.
In proposing this motion the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis) said that the Senate has protected Canadians. I wish a speaker in this House would come up with a concrete example which contains any degree of agreement on other than the most slender of partisan pretences. The fact is that, be the power of appointment with the provincial governments or with the federal Government, it is still a patronage power of appointment. Nothing in this resolution would lay upon Senators any responsibility to attend and participate in committee meetings.
I would like to take a moment to praise those members of the Senate who do attend and participate in committee meetings. Many of them make a valuable contribution. However, that does not mean that the institution itself should persist unchanged.
The alternative of provincial patronage might seem satisfactory to some. It would, after all, involve a distribution, a devolution if you like, of the patronage powers. These are the usual arguments that we have heard for the Senate alternatives that come up. Unfortunately, although some of them have a certain mathematical elegance, they overwhelmingly lack the characteristic of democratic participation except, of course, when an elected Senate is called for. All those arguments and schemes essentially ignore the terrible opportunities for conflict and dissension which could occur if there were an elected upper chamber setting itself against the will of the people as expressed in the election of the House of Commons.
Senate Reform
I am confident that this resolution will go down to defeat. It always interests me to see another scheme for Senate reform but, overwhelmingly, this is not what Canadians want. If any Government were to put the fate of the Senate to Canadians in a referendum, we would have a unicameral Parliament in this country.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867-1982-REFORM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the resolution proposed today by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis) is a most interesting one. It reflects the Hon. Member's abiding interest in parliamentary reform and the depth of his thinking on this subject.
This resolution could open the doors of the Senate to improved regional representation by allowing the provincial Governments to appoint half of the senators representing them. The concept of the Senate as a "Council of Confederation" is not a new one. Many Senate reform proposals, including the more ambitious ones, have recommended some form of provincial representation. The pros and cons of this idea would merit careful consideration by this House, and although that is not the purpose of my speech today, I am sure one of my colleagues will raise this issue.
Madam Speaker, today I would like to draw the attention of the House to the second aspect of the proposal now being considered. It concerns the legislative process proposed by the Hon. Member and the power the Senate would have as a result.
According to the resolution, when a Bill is adopted by one Chamber and voted down by the other, Parliament would set up a mediation committee consisting of representatives of both Chambers and based on the proportion of seats each party has in the House of Commons. The proposal by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings implies that the committee would examine the Bill with a view to either smoothing out or reflecting the differences between Senators and Members and reaching a common position. The Hon. Member's proposal concludes, and I quote:
That, where a conference committee proposal fails to be adopted by both
Houses, the original bill be withdrawn.
It follows, Madam Speaker, that this would confirm the Senate's veto right over all actions of Parliament, as stated in the Constitution Act, 1867, a veto right that is no longer exercised today.
This constitutes the originality of the Hon. Member's proposal. None of the major Senate reform plans over the last twenty years recommends maintaining the absolute veto right of a Senate appointed either by the provinces, the federal Government or both. To those in favour of an elected Senate, only the proposal released by the Government of Prince Edward Island in 1983, confirms the legislative powers exercised by the Senate since 1867 while maintaining the Senate's absolute veto right.
None of the parliamentary proposals, including those by the senators themselves, and none of the federal Government's

March 19, 1987
Senate Reform
proposals have suggested that all the Senate's powers should be preserved. In fact, they recommended restricting those powers.
In its 1972 report the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution of Canada maintained practically unchanged the current system of appointment and the right of the Senate to study proposed legislation. However it did limit the Senate veto to imposing a six-month delay on any bill which would not have the full support of the Upper House. Then the House of Commons would simply have had to pass a new bill to reverse the unfavourable Senate decision and thus get the legislative process rolling again. On this question, Madam Speaker, Hon. Members and senators of the committee concluded:
In the case of the Senate a curbing of its veto power would, paradoxically, strengthen it, and do so without weakening the House of Commons. It would increase the possibilities of confrontation, but avoid the perpetuation of deadlock by ultimately giving the House of Commons its way.
Under the 1978 bill on constitutional reform, the famous Bill C-60, it was proposed to turn the Senate into a House of the Federation, half it members being appointed by the House of Commons, the other half by the various legislative assemblies. This measure is not far removed from the Hon. Member's resolution. However it takes a totally different approach with respect to the absolute veto which would apply exclusively to the approval of appointments to the Supreme Court and senior positions of certain federal organizations. On most other issues the Senate would have had only a 60-day suspensive veto, after which the controversial measure could have been submitted to the Governor General without the House of Commons having to reconsider its position. The only exception had to do with legislation of a linguistic character or of federal-provincial importance. In both cases a Senate refusal could have been reversed only through a favourable vote by two thirds of the House of Commons.
As you can see, Madam Speaker, we are still a long way from the absolute veto over all legislative measures, as advocated by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings.
In 1980, the Senate Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs also looked at Senate reform. In its report on some of the aspects of the Canadian Constitution, better known as the Goldenberg-Lamontagne Report, that committee recommended that the Senate be given a suspensive veto of a maximum of six months, after which the House of Commons would have to pass for a second time legislative measures that would have been rejected. According to that committee, such a delay and the requirement for a new debate in the House of Commons would allow the general public to be alerted and to make the necessary pressures to protect their interests.
Furthermore, those senators, who would themselves be the first affected by Senate reform, have rejected the idea of the absolute veto which they now have, for the reason that, in a democratic society, such powers could not be vested in a Chamber whose Members are appointed. The use of the
absolute veto, according to those senators, would be tantamount to violating the will of the people.
More recently, the Joint Special Committee on Senate Reform, in its January 1984 report, came to the conclusion that an elected Senate was the best means of giving the Upper Chamber the required political authority.
That committee, Madam Speaker, also refused to maintain the Senate's absolute veto, even if it were an elected Senate, thereby empowered by the nation's will. In that respect, the committee wrote: "The principal factor in our decision not to accord the Senate an absolute veto was the possibility, if not the probability, of our parliamentary institutions continually becoming deadlocked. We therefore decided that it was wiser and more in keeping with the character of parliamentary government to give the Senate the power to delay but not altogether prevent the adoption of measures voted by the House of Commons."
The report therefore recommended a suspensive veto of a maximum of 120 sitting days. This means that bills rejected by the Senate within the 60 sitting days following their transmission to that House, according to that formula, would have to be passed by the House of Commons a second time. That second adoption could not take place unless at least 60 sitting days has elapsed since the Senate rejected the bill. Therefore, that formula could enable the Senate to delay for a number of months the implementation of a bill it felt was unaceptable, but could not enable it to cripple the Commons and the Government.
However, this did not appear to be enough to eliminate the absolute veto, and the 1984 Joint Committee wanted to further restrict the powers of the Senate by limiting the use of the suspensive veto by exempting all supply bills. On that matter, the Committee wrote: "To give the Senate even a suspensive veto in such a vital area would amount to giving it a disguised power to overturn the government. We therefore propose that the Senate have no power over appropriation bills (including the main, interim and supplementary estimates)."
The only case where the Committee judged it appropriate to maintain the absolute veto of the Senate was the adoption of bills or parts of bills with a linguistic significance. To give the French linguistic and cultural minority a fair over-representation on matters which directly concern them, the Committee had recommended that any legislation of linguistic significance be approved by a majority of all Senators including a majority of the francophone Senators. In the 1984 report, this was the only instance where it was recommended to maintain the absolute veto held by the Senate since 1867.
As you can see, Madam Speaker, each time that Parliament and the Federal Government have examined Senate reform in the last 15 years, it has been recommended that the absolute veto be eliminated. Whether the reform proposed was for an appointed Senate, an assembly of provincial delegations or an elected Chamber, whether it was on the basis of legitimacy or government efficiency, it has in each case been recommended
March 19, 1987

that the powers of the Senate be restricted to a suspensive veto on the great majority of legislative measures. Most proposals by provincial Governments and groups interested in this issue, most if not all of the proposals made in the last 20 years, have recommended the same thing.
Madam Speaker, the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings is an exception to the rule. By maintaining for the Senate powers identical to those of the House of Commons, this motion puts the appointed Chamber in direct competition with the elected Chamber. In the motion, only trust in the good faith of parliamentarians guarantees that the will of the population as expressed by its elected representatives will prevail in case of a deadlock. I admire this trust of the Hon. Member in the good faith of parliamentarians, but I am afraid that it will not be enough to protect us from frequent stoppages of the legislative process. In my opinion, the proposal would be more credible if it provided for an unblocking mechanism such as a suspensive veto.
I ask my colleagues in this House to reflect on this aspect of the matter before deciding whether to support this motion today.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867-1982-REFORM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I commend the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis) for bringing an extremely important subject to the floor of the House of Commons.
In 1975 the Hon. Member came to speak in my riding, and I have been elected four times since. If he comes to my constituency again and talks about Senate reform, I could get elected another four times.
There is probably no place in Canada which has more of a grass roots, broadly spread desire for changes to the Senate than has the Province of Alberta. This came about because of a bleeding away from that province of some S30 billion as a result of the Liberal National Energy Program. It brought about a sense of anger which is so deep-rooted in Alberta that today it believes the only way in which it will be able to sustain a sense of fairness in Confederation is with a reformed Senate.
Another observation I want to make-and I make it particularly as a result of the comments of the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry)-is that indeed this country is naive if we are of the presumption that there are no problems among our regions. In fact, I find it surprising that a Member from northern Ontario would not want some sense of regional balance in a federal system.
Although my good friend, the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings, would have some differences of view in respect of the specifics of a reformed Senate, I want to start out by saying how much I commend him for introducing the idea in the House of Commons. I believe that political bodies ought to be elected. I know that that view differs from the views of others in the House, and those views are legitimately
Senate Reform
held, but I believe they ought to be elected. As was the case with the Magna Carta some 700 years ago, the whole purpose of politics in a democracy is for the people to have a sense of power. That cannot come about unless the citizens believe that their representatives are elected and that they have a chance to put them in and a chance to throw the rascals out. That sense of power must be present.
Let us take a look at Canada. It is about 4.5 thousand miles wide. Its population is largely concentrated within 100 miles of the American border, a ribbon which stretches from Vancouver Island to Prince Edward Island. There are more Members of Parliament from the urban areas of Toronto and Montreal than there are from Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Yukon, Northwest Territories, and two-thirds of British Columbia, northern British Columbia. In other words, two cities outnumber about 75 per cent of Canada's land mass. Surely that signals the need for regional balance in political decision making.
I do not want to recite an old adage which demonstrates triteness, partly because I cannot remember it just now. However, we have all heard that fine saying that if we destroy the cities, the hinterland will develop new cities, and that if we destroy the hinterland, the grasses will grow in our cities. I simply say to you, Madam Speaker, that all that a city is is a processor of the hinterland. It does nothing else except manufacture what it takes from the hinterland. It ensures that what is taken out of the hinterland can be manufactured for resale to those in that area of the country. I do not use the word hinterland in any derogatory way. I am very proud because that is the resource base-the fish, the lumber, the minerals, the like.
.
I believe that if there is a concern that we ought to be reflecting upon today, it is that concern that arises from the void that existed in this country in the mid-1970s because we had no Senate with any effective power. The Government of the day began the process of institutionalizing First Ministers' Conferences. Premiers began to fill that gap that the Senate had or ought to have filled.
The result of the proposed process, as I see it, is that the Senate would simply be appointed by provinces or a federal Government. I hold that that would do away with what I think this country is aching for, namely, a federal system for which the citizens of the country could have and respect. There is a thirst within Canada to want to be Canadian, irrespective of whether one is from New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan or the Territories. We want a federal system that works.
We have heard a lot in western Canada about a "triple E" Senate, one "E" to mean elected. That I accept because I accept that power should be with the people. The other "E" is equal. On that I want to expand for just a moment because I am a product of six years of university in the United States. I recognized that in America little Rhode Island had two

March 19, 1987
Senate Reform
Senators to offset two Senators from California. Great big heavily populated New York had two Senators to offset 500,000 or 600,000 persons in Wyoming which had two Senators.
Frequently in the U.S. people talk about "us" and "we" while Canadians have this all too often tendency to talk about "I" and "them", pointing at each other across the map. Yet I submit there is less difference between a person from Dallas and one from Boston than there is between a person from Edmonton and one from Toronto. Perhaps that reflects the fact that we do not have within any federal institution a sense that we all have some equal partnership in our federation. I believe that equality is also important.
I might add, parenthetically, one other observation, Madam Speaker. Let me refer to United States Senators Dave Church, a former Senator from Idaho, Mike Mansfield, again a former Senator who used to be the Senate majority leader, and Senator Barry Goldwater of whom we have all heard. The Senators who had prominent positions were the ones who came from the smallest populated states because that was part of the unwritten law, and it brought a sense of equality.
My final point is that of effectiveness, Madam Speaker. That is where I believe the institution ought to be measured in its judgment and that is what the real debate is about. It is important that we have a Senate that is elected, that is equal, but probably with some measure of control so that it could not always force one vote by one person to reverse House of Commons legislation. This would mean it could have sober second thought and it could demand another reflection. If that were so, I think the citizens of the nation by and large would send to the House of Commons the necessary signals to bring the balance we need in debate in this place.
I see that my time is up, Madam Speaker. I want to conclude by thanking the Hon. Member for Prince Edward- Hastings for bringing such an important Bill to our attention.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION ACTS 1867-1982-REFORM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the few minutes remaining in private Members' hour, I welcome this opportunity to participate in the debate on the motion sponsored by a very distinguished private Member of this House, the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis). His motion has given us an opportunity today to look at the broad issue of Senate reform, a subject that has received considerable attention over the years, probably starting on July 2, 1867.
The Prime Minister of that day, our first Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, coined the phrase "sober second thought". I think it is clear, although it is certainly a moot point, that from Confederation to the present day the Senate has made an important contribution in the area of legislative review. But the Fathers of Confederation also intended that the Senate should have a regional representation function. They used the expression "sectional interests" as being protected. I think few of us would deny that the second
principle function intended for the Senate is not being carried out effectively.
Why is it that the Senate is not able to play an effective role in regional representation? Again, there is broad agreement in this House, and I think across the country, that for Senators to be appointed by the federal Government until age 75 lessens the ability of Senators to represent their regions. As pointed out by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), the public does not accord a high level of legitimacy to Senators, largely because of the appointment method. As a result, the Senate lacks the authority to exercise the substantial powers it has under the Constitution. I think the Senators themselves, however willing and able they might be, are not seen as defending regional interests.
It seems quite clear that the principle purpose behind many recent proposals for Senate reform has been to restore to that chamber its intended role in regional representation. That is certainly one of the main aims of the Hon. Member from Prince Edward-Hastings. Some have pointed out that in the absence of a sufficiently strong second chamber, provincial Governments and Premiers have, on occasion, stepped in to try to fill that gap. Others have observed that our electoral system has created the impression that the support for national political Parties in particular regions is much lower than it really is. They also point out that in its present form the Senate cannot help to compensate for the imbalances in elected representation in this House.
There are other arguments for an enhanced regional representation role for the Senate, but in the end most of them share a common goal, to allow Canada's Senate to play the sort of role that second chambers play in other federal systems.
What is the evidence that improved regional representation has become the main focus of Senate reform proposals? I would suggest there is a substantial body of evidence to this effect, Madam Speaker. The former Special Joint Committee on Senate Reform was asked in its terms of reference, for example, to:
Report on ways by which the Senate of Canada could be reformed in order to strengthen its role in representing people from all regions of Canada.
The committee, as you know, heard many witnesses from various regions and sectors of Canadian society. Although their views and proposals differed, it is fair to say that more witnesses called for the Senate's regional representation role to be strengthened than for any other function to be emphasized.
In the remaining minute or so I would like to refer to one witness, a strong representative from western Canada, Dr. David Elton, President of the Canada West Foundation who said:
In this country what we really need are regional spokesmen in Ottawa, not provincial Governments per se, but regional spokesmen who can address the concerns of their constituents and ensure that they have a meaningful role to play in the deliberation and the legislation that the national Government brings into existence.
I appreciate that my time has expired and I thank the House for its attention, Madam Speaker.
March 19, 1987

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-GOVERNMENT POSITION-DEMAND FOR DETAILED INFORMATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last Friday, or last week in any case, I rose in the House to raise a matter I felt was important. I wanted to shed some light on the sale of certain federal services, more specifically the Surveys and Mapping Services and the Canada Centre for Remote Sensing at the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, and the Canadian Hydrographic Survey at Fisheries and Oceans. The House will recall that the issue raised quite a few comments for about ten days, and that finally, the Government put an end to the debate in the House by giving us the whole truth, saying it had no intention of privatizing these services which were judged to be essential.
The main point of my intervention at the time consisted in showing that the Government was sometimes hard-pressed to be clear to Canadians about its intentions and how it would proceed. Anyone who did not keep track of the Government's record in this debate might have thought this was an exception, an isolated incident, but it seems to be a pattern, a scenario that is being repeated time and time again.
This evening, I would like to raise a matter which I think will be of considerable interest to Hon. Members, and on which this Government is still hesitating and dragging its feet. I am referring to the Official Languages Act and the promise made by this Government in two Throne Speeches and during the 1984 election campaign. It has been said repeatedly in this House, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and by the responsible Ministers, including the Secretary of State, the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Justice, that the Government intends to table amendments to the Official Languages Act. The latest question on the subject, Madam Speaker, which is the subject of my speech this
Adjournment Debate
evening, goes back to December 11, 1986, at page 2022 of Hansard.
The Official Languages Act has been in existence for nearly seventeen years. As so many of us, it is showing its age, and needs some improvements. It needs to be modernized, to be updated, to reflect today's reality, and I do not think I know a single Member of this House who is against the suggestion, as I said, that the legislation be brought before this forum, this Parliament so that we might update it, strengthen it and amend it as required.
And this is becoming urgent because mentalities have changed in Canada since it was adopted in 1969. We must admit indeed that the situation has changed. The Constitution was repatriated and it has brought on many significant changes concerning the whole linguistic issue, and there have been a number of judgments by various Canadian courts about the interpretation to be given to both the Constitution and the Official Languages Act.
The result of all this is that we need leadership, we need amendments to the Official Languages Act. I think it is imperative that the matter be dealt with by the House, that the Government show leadership and, as I said earlier, that it find solutions to the important questions of national culture and identity, that it give a new spirit, if you like, a new vigour to the Official Languages Act and its application.
Madam Speaker, basic reforms are a must if we want to meet the challenges of the years 2000. A whole new generation has been raised in this atmosphere, this new climate, this new way of thinking and seeing things.
I believe that this generation is increasingly willing to accept both Canadian realities and to accept that they can flourish without either one being threatened. I do not believe that anyone could demonstrate today that, by asserting my rights as a francophone, I could in any way weaken or diminish the rights of the English-speaking majority, and vice versa, in Quebec, I do not believe that an English-speaking Canadian who asserts his right to use his own language at home can threaten in any way the identity or right to exist of the Quebec majority.
Madam Speaker, I am not alone in saying that it is essential to amend the Official Languages Act. As I have already pointed out, the Prime Minister has repeated on many occasions in the House and during the electoral campaign, and the Government has given Canadians hope in two Speeches from the Throne that this legislation will be amended. Until now, we have heard only promises and endless excuses, but as we all know, Madam Speaker, there are limits to anyone's patience, and I believe that the Government should now set some time table for the Canadian public and announce what will be done about the linguistic issue. The Government should introduce amendments as soon as possible during this session so that we may look at them and discuss them with our usual openmindedness. Such a process can only lead to a piece of

March 19, 1987
Adjournment Debate
legislation which will be much more appropriate to this day and age.
We must not hesitate too long because to do so could lead to other instances of what we saw in the case of the RCMP. Certain agencies could use such an opportunity to make undesirable changes by saying that there is a vacuum which must be filled. I want to invite the Parliamentary Secretary, in the spirit of reform and to show that this Government and this Parliament speak for all Canadians, to give to all the Government agencies which might be somewhat impatient and want to take action a firm and specific indication this evening that amendments will be introduced in the near future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-GOVERNMENT POSITION-DEMAND FOR DETAILED INFORMATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is on behalf of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) tonight that I am providing details on the questions raised by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). First, Madam Speaker, concerning the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, as the President of the Treasury Board already indicated, the Treasury Board has neither considered nor approved of any reduction for whatever reason in the RCMP's or any other federal institution's goals for hiring employees or recruits whose first official language is French. Policy changes proposed by the RCMP in that respect will be submitted to his colleagues in the Treasury Board and to himself for consideration.
With respect to the many complaints that were filed with the Commissioner of Official Languages against the Canadian Security Intelligence service, as was mentioned by my colleague the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher) here some time ago, action already has been taken to remedy the situation. This action includes the appointment of a larger number of bilingual officers at headquarters, the enhancement of language skills for certain key positions, as well as an increase in the envelope for translation, in order that written communications be provided in both official languages.
As far as language training is concerned, the expected Public Service Commission staff reductions will not lead to any reduction in the use of French in Government Departments because, wherever possible, language teachers will be moved to other positions within the Public Service itself. On the contrary, changes to the language training policy and staff restructuring within the Public Service Commission are a major initiative in terms of efficiency and effectiveness in the area of official languages. As Hon. Members know, the Government will still be picking up the costs of language training needed for operational requirements, and also encouraging language training with a view to improving individual career prospects. Training opportunities will not be reduced, neither inside departments nor regarding the employees.
As to the question of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier concerning the presentation of the Bill amending the Official
Languages Act, I cannot but repeat the statement the Prime Minister made on that subject on the 5th of December last year. If it is not before Christmas, it will be shortly after, due to the consultations the Government absolutely wants to hold on that matter.
Finally, Madam Speaker, the Government is well aware of the necessity to increase the francophone representation among the administrative group. You can rest assured that it spares no effort to that end. Along with the Public Service Commission, the Treasury Board keeps a watchful eye on the matter. Given the circumstances, of course, it may still take a few years before we reach a completely satisfactory situation, but the President of the Treasury Board wants you to know that this principle is of the utmost importance for the Government, and that all fair measures are taken, while respecting the merit principle, in order to continue increasing the francophone representation in the administrative group of the federal Public Service.

subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-OPPORTUNITY TO INCREASE FUNDS FOR RESEARCH. (B) APPROVAL OF PROJECTS
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-OPPORTUNITY TO INCREASE FUNDS FOR RESEARCH. (B) APPROVAL OF PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in preparing for my remarks this evening I was reminded of a comment made by John Polanyi, the Nobel laureate, at a dinner in his honour in Ottawa several weeks ago. A video tape had been shown, touching on some of the highlights of his remarkable career. In characteristically modest fashion, Professor Polanyi said that his work was but an element of the story of Canadian achievement past, present and future. "The question is", he said, "how long will that future be postponed"?
Canadians are still waiting for an answer to that question from the Conservative Government. Indeed, all we have seen since the last election are reversals and confusion, a policy and a Government that is in disarray. The saga of Canada's participation in the space station is a perfect illustration of a policy and a Government in disarray.
When I asked my question regarding cuts at the National Research Council, the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) denied for the umpteenth time that there had been any cuts at the National Research Council. Who did the Minister think he was fooling? Surely not the small businesses in Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan that I visited in September and October, prior to the announcement of the cuts. They told me that their projects had been put on hold because of a lack of funding in the Industrial Research Assistance Program, which is one of the most effective government programs in helping small and mediumsized businesses across Canada to do research and become innovative.
The truth is that the Cabinet ordered a cut in that program. However, the Minister had to back down following a wave of protest from across the country and when the members of the
March 19, 1987

board of directors of the National Research Council refused to take that direction from the Government to cut IRAP.
While the Government announced its participation in the space station over a year ago, we still do not know today where the money is coming from to pay for that program. We know that the National Research Council was forced to contribute some S60 million. The Minister was asked by an Ottawa Citizen reporter last fall to provide a list of the exact sources of money. Tie declined to do so because, he said: "It might cause my colleagues at other Departments unnecessary problems".
We have had a hint of some of these problems in recent days. We have learned that regional development moneys will go into the space program. Indeed, the Cabinet has ordered the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion to take some $35 million and $5 million respectively, or a total of $40 million, from the Laprade Fund and the Lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe Funds to pay for our participation in the space program.
[ Translation]
Madam Speaker, not a single cent of that money will go back to the Mauricie, Bois-Francs or Gaspe areas, because there are no opportunities there. There is no research facilities and there is no way that part of the country can participate in the space program. Consequently, funds that had been earmarked by the Government for regional development are being secretly taken away, without the Government telling the truth to the Canadian population.
I mentioned this to the Minister several weeks ago and he expressed surprise that we had obtained the information. He wondered how we had got it. A researcher from the Library of Parliament got it through a simple telephone call to the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. The Minister really outdid himself in answering a question I put to him two weeks ago. I again asked him when he would be able to provide us with details of the funding of the space program. He replied: "I do not know if I will ever be able to provide such information, if I will ever know what the answers are". Does that not inspire confidence in the Government? Canadians can really sleep well tonight knowing that our Government is in such good hands.
Professor Polanyi was once again disappointed by the Government when it announced its science and technology strategy 10 days ago. Our future is still on hold. I do not know if you have seen this policy statement, Madam Speaker. It is a very fancy policy statement. It looks like a placemat. It is pretty. It has the coats of arms of the provincial and territorial Governments. It has the signatures of the Ministers, but there is not one more nickel for research funds. I hope that one of these days the Government will learn that what we need is more spending for research, not cutting. The Minister will
Adjournment Debate
learn that we cannot solve problems by throwing promises endlessly at them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-OPPORTUNITY TO INCREASE FUNDS FOR RESEARCH. (B) APPROVAL OF PROJECTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as usual, the Hon. Member has departed from the question he asked and it is really annoying. The question he asked was why the Government has reduced IRAP funding by $60 million, thereby jeopardizing the competitiveness of Canadian industry, particularly small and medium-size business. The Hon. Member did not deal with that question at all, and that is what he asked.
I am pleased to respond today because it provides the opportunity to set the record straight on this issue. Simply, the Government never cut the NRC IRAP Program by $60 million. The Hon. Member should know that the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) gave his personal assurances that the level of IRAP grants in 1986-87 would not be any less than in previous years.
As the Hon. Member is so poorly informed about federal science and technology policy, perhaps he will not mind if I take a moment to educate him. Let me first say that the Government's actions with respect to the NRC have been part of a consistent policy. The Speech from the Throne announced the opening of a major effort to carve out a significant place for science and technology in the culture of Canada.
Had we taken office with a clean slate, there would have been few problems in meeting these objectives. Instead, we inherited a crisis situation which was built up by the Party to which the Hon. Member belongs. Years of unrealistic spending has led to an intolerable deficit position. Federal science and technology expenditures were an unco-ordinated grab-bag of programs, many just bricks and mortar, not science, working in isolation and often at cross-purposes. This meant that we could not move as freely or as quickly as we wanted. In particular, we found that the federal Government science and technology effort was in poor shape. There was no consistent national science and technology policy or priorities. As a result, the efforts of federal agencies, provincial organizations, universities and industry were unco-ordinated and, at times, ineffective. Funding for the granting councils was not secure, and vast sums were being spent on additional bricks and mortar for various federal facilities. Finally, the scientific research tax credit was losing significant tax revenue with little result.
Since taking office the Government has worked on four different fronts. First, we halted the SRTCs and replaced them with a refundable tax credit designed to help all Canadian companies, especially small start-up firms. Second, we have given the granting councils a guaranteed funding base for the next five years. From this measure alone, the university research community could receive over $ 1 billion in additional funds over the next five years. Third, we have developed a national consensus on science and technology that fully

March 19, 1987
Adjournment Debate
involves all players. The product of this consensus building, which has recently been announced by the Minister of State for Science and Technology in Vancouver, is a national science and technology policy setting out the framework for a more coordinated and vigorous national effort in R and D. Fourth, we have begun to rationalize the Government's laboratories system, including NRC, to focus federal efforts on support to industry.
All these measures have been put in place within the constraints imposed by the deficit position. Despite these constraints the Government is finding additional resources when requested by NRC to meet new requirements. In fact, NRC is getting an additional 62 person-years for its operations next year.
In summary, the situation at NRC has been misrepresented and exaggerated out of all proportion by the Opposition. In actual fact the reductions which have taken place were necessary but very limited. The impact on people is being contained and the NRC remains a strong and viable research facility with new resources in important areas such as biotechnology.

ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-FORTHCOMING MEETING BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND UNITED STATES PRESIDENT. (B) NEED FOR UNITED STATES COMMITMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as you well know, the subject I raise tonight is with respect to acid rain. It is becoming evident that the Government's acid rain strategy is falling apart. We have now reached a stage at which getting President Reagan to live up to a commitment made a year ago has been proclaimed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to be a very significant movement. The fact of the matter is we are now locked into a five-year research and demonstration program. This is a program that will have no benefits to our dying lakes, forests and ecosystem because there are no commitments within the program to cut acid rain.
As Michael Perley of the Canadian Coalition on Acid Rain put it:
Clean coal technology isn't the key to the solution ... Emission reduction is
the key.
I ask myself and the Parliamentary Secretary what the Prime Minister will be bargaining for at the summit on April 5 since he accepted with open arms yesterday President Reagan's proposed solution with respect to continuing with more demonstration projects. Not only has the Prime Minister accepted it, he has done so three weeks before the summit begins. Thus he has basically given away any bargaining position that he might have had. He could have remained silent and prepared on the basis of a position for Canada that would go well beyond what was announced yesterday in Washington by President Reagan. One has to ask oneself what the Prime Minister will be asking at the summit now that he has said: "Hurrah, that is what we want". Yet it was something promised a year ago, and it was for more than demonstration and research.
I ask the Parliamentary Secretary when the Government will muster the necessary courage-and not very much is needed-to say in a straightforward and plain manner to President Reagan that what we want is not more research and demonstration but cuts in acid rain. We want a significant program from the Canadian point of view with deadlines, percentages and dates such as we have launched on the Canadian side. We want to move ahead together in the interests of Americans and Canadians. One begins to wonder why the Government is pussyfooting around instead of saying it as it is. The basic mistake was made a year or two ago when this Envoy's report was launched and it was decided that we should go for research and development. Time is running out. Years are going by and the environment is still subject to deterioration and constant acidic precipitation.
We are not alone in saying this. Henry Wexman, the U.S. representative in Congress, says that by accepting President Reagan's pledge our Prime Minister has been accused of "selling out the Canadian people and the Canadian environment". He went on to say, "I am surprised that the second time around the Prime Minister would not see through the President's hocus-pocus . . . This is a betrayal of our common environment".
As another example, Clifford Lincoln, the Quebec Minister of the Environment, said Reagan's promise "sounds good until you read between the lines. There's nothing about limits of reduction. There's nothing about abatements. There's nothing about timetables. The signal is very clear to us. We've got to start pushing and screaming a little louder". That is what a distinguished Minister of the Environment in Canada is saying.
If that is not enough, Senator George Mitchell, the Chairman of the U.S. Senate Subcommittee on the Environment, said last week: "I hope the same thing does not happen again", namely this acceptance by the Prime Minister of President Reagan's diplomatic solutions. Madam Speaker, of course questions are important but sometimes the answers are also. One must surely have to be quite bold to ask such a question and challenge us about our achievements. When one really considers what we have done . . . This Government, Madam Speaker, has done more to solve the problem of acid rain-and besides it has been recognized by everyone including the media-than the previous Governement.
March 19, 1987

The Prime Minister met with President Reagan in Quebec City in March 1986. They decided to conclude an agreement. During that time, the Opposition was chuckling and laughing and still was looking for dirt and scandals.
Then, Madam Speaker, the representatives appointed by the United States and Canada met to discuss acid rain and means to solve the problems. They came up with recommendations and findings. The U.S. President and Mr. Mulroney met in Washington in March 1986, one year later. They accepted those findings and promised to take the necesssary action. During that time, our opponents on the other side were still looking for dirt and scandals. They were not making any comparison with what had been done in past years.
Today, Madam Speaker, my colleague for Richmond- Wolfe (Mr. Tardif), a Member of the party opposite, has risen in the House to address the disastrous effects of acid rain on maple trees and said that conditions will be worse four years from now. I fully agree with him and I find it terrible. The people in my Beauharnois-Salaberry riding agree. However, Madam Speaker, acid rain is not the result of the election of a Tory Government in September 1984. The problems did not happen overnight after the election of the Tories. What was done before Septembre 1984 in that regard? If these problems
Adjournment Debate
are so catastrophic as is the case today, it is because absolutely nothing was done in the past. Do you know what he proposed for a solution? Will the producers receive any money? That is what has always been done. They think money can buy them peace of mind. That is not the solution. We have to take the proper means.
The last announcement.. . Mr. Bush did indeed come here, Madam Speaker, when we indicated how concerned we were about the agreement that was signed with Mexico; he took the trouble to come here in person. It did not happen when the Members opposite were in government. They were still scouring the garbage cans for scandals. What happened last Wednesday in Washington? Funds were allocated. Let us trust people who are sane and who wish to build a better world as fast as they can.
